newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Mr Nyet makes govt, now he could break it.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Mr Nyet makes govt, now he could break it.

text.p: A year ago, Marxist leader Fausto Bertinotti was trumpeting his role as king-maker for helping Italy's left into government for the first time in 50 years.
On Wednesday, Bertinotti was "Mr Nyet", after his refusal to back the government in a vote on a security force for Albania put Prime Minister Romano Prodi's future on the line.
Commentators struggled to see how Prodi's centre-left coalition, which needs support from Communist Refoundation for a parliamentary majority, could rebuild the shattered alliance.

Prodi appeared to have staved off an immediate crisis over the U.N.-approved security mission, due to start deploying next week to protect relief shipments for lawless Albania, after an 11th hour deal with the opposition to vote on a joint motion.

But some commentators said nothing short of divine intervention may be needed to mop up the political mess left by Bertinotti's ideological mutiny as government partners demanded a showdown with Refoundation.
"The government would be left with the task, or rather the miracle, of resurrecting itself," La Repubblica newspaper said.

Prodi's coalition partners have made clear that the government cannot continue to be held hostage by Bertinotti, whose party commands less than 10 percent of the vote but holds the balance of power with 34 deputies in the lower house.
Bertinotti, a mild-mannered 57-year-old former trades unionist, has nothing evident to gain from a government collapse that would be sure to diminish his party's influence.
"If this government falls, it won't be our fault," he told Corriere della Sera newspaper.

He agreed that it would mean a wasted opportunity for the left, locked out of power for decades in Italy, but insisted it would be the fault of Prodi and his partners for "not having had the courage to build a government really capable of change".
Refoundation, formed in 1991 by a few hardliners when the West's mightiest communist party relaunched as a social democratic force, disagreed with Prodi from day one.
It wasted no time in issuing a string of demands for the government's first 100 days in office that clashed with the policies of Prodi, an economist from the political centre.

Prodi, worn out by battles with Refoundation over economic policy, tough budgetary measures, unemployment, privatisation, welfare state reform and a European single currency, acknowledged last month that Refoundation was a hindrance.
"It's clear that without Refoundation we'd have achieved more," he told Spanish daily El Pais in an interview.
Bertinotti, the dapper son of a socialist railway worker, makes no apologies for his inflexibility, saying that being on the left meant being committed to social and employment issues.

In his trademark calm and courteous fashion, he has already served notice of a refusal to compromise on what he has called the "mother of all questions -- the welfare state", which he says will really put Prodi's government to the test.

Italy, struggling to keep a tight lid on spending in a bid to join the European single currency at its launch in 1999, is preparing to review its social security system. Bertinotti vehemently opposes any cuts.
